passage:
Subject: Something at work
Dear Naveen,
When we worked on the audit team you told me to write if things got difficult, so here goes. On Monday, in the review with the regional head and five others, my senior, Mr Kulkarni, presented the pricing model I built as “my approach.” He looked at the slide the whole time and never at me. I said nothing. I sat there with my face hot, angry and strangely helpless. Afterwards two colleagues quietly told me they knew it was mine, but nobody spoke in the meeting. I don't want to confront him in public. I've started a dated file of what I contribute, and I'll show him the next draft early with a short note to the team. Does that sound sensible?
Disha

qa.q: What did Mr Kulkarni call the pricing model in the review?
What was Disha feeling as Disha sat through the review?
qa.a: Disha felt angry and helpless, with a hot face, and stayed silent in front of the regional head and five others.

qa.q: What steps does Disha plan instead of a public confrontation?
qa.a: Disha has started a dated file of contributions and plans to show the next draft early with a short note to the team.

qa.q: How might the two colleagues who quietly said they knew it was Disha's have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt uneasy about not speaking up in the meeting, which fits telling Disha afterwards in private.

grounding: A junior finds their work presented as a senior's idea, feels anger and helplessness and chooses to document contributions and speak early.

passage: So, the worst moment? Honestly, a Wednesday. I'm Lavanya, and I had spent three weekends on a customer-survey design. In the client call, my manager Ganga said, “Here is the approach I've developed,” and clicked to my slide. Seven people on that call, and nobody looked at me because nobody knew it was mine. I was so angry my hands went cold, and I couldn't think of a single thing to say that wouldn't sound petty. That night I emailed myself the dates and drafts. From then on my weekly update named exactly what I was working on, and in the next planning meeting I spoke early: “I'll present the survey design.” Ganga blinked, then said, “Good. Go ahead.”

qa.q: How many people were on the client call?
qa.a: Seven people were on the call.

qa.q: Why couldn't Lavanya think of anything to say during the call?
qa.a: Lavanya was so angry that hands went cold, and feared that anything said would sound petty in front of the client.

qa.q: What did Lavanya change after that night, and why was it a safer choice than confronting in public?
qa.a: Lavanya kept dated records, named the work in the weekly update and claimed the presentation early, which made ownership clear without embarrassing Ganga in front of a client.

qa.q: What might Ganga have been thinking when Ganga blinked at Lavanya's early claim?
qa.a: Ganga was probably surprised and may have realised that Lavanya's work was now visible, so agreeing with “Good. Go ahead.” was the easy way to respond.

grounding: A junior finds their work presented as a senior's idea, feels anger and helplessness and chooses to document and speak up early.
